nameStory: This tiny fungus gets its name from the Greek words 'chloros' meaning green and 'splenium' meaning bandage or patch, perfectly describing its appearance as small green patches on wood. The species name 'chlora' doubles down on the green theme, making this one of the most aptly named fungi you'll encounter. It's sometimes called the Green Wood Cup, though the 'cups' are so small you might mistake them for green paint splatters at first glance.
description: Green Wood Cup is a tiny fungus that forms brilliant blue-green to yellow-green patches on decaying hardwood logs and branches. Each individual fruiting body is cup-shaped but incredibly small - usually just 1-3 millimeters across, about the size of a pinhead. When many grow together, they create conspicuous bright green patches that can span several inches across the wood surface. This is one of the few fungi that's truly green in color, making it quite distinctive once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Vivid green color
idTips.description: Unmistakable bright blue-green to yellow-green color that looks almost artificial, like someone dabbed green paint on the wood

idTips.label: Tiny cup shape
idTips.description: Individual cups are pinhead-sized but visible to naked eye, feeling smooth and slightly rubbery when fresh

idTips.label: Clustered patches
idTips.description: Grows in dense colonies that form irregular bright green patches several inches across on wood surfaces

idTips.label: Hardwood host
idTips.description: Always found on decaying deciduous wood, never on conifers - feels soft and punky under the fungus

idTips.label: Smooth surface
idTips.description: Cup interior is completely smooth without any wrinkles, ridges, or hair-like structures when examined closely

habitat: Found exclusively on decaying hardwood logs, branches, and stumps in moist forest environments throughout New England. Prefers well-rotted wood that's soft and spongy, often in shaded areas near streams or in humid valley bottoms. Commonly appears on oak, maple, beech, and birch wood that's been down for at least a year or two.

seasonality.spring: Fresh bright green patches begin appearing on logs as temperatures warm and humidity increases. This is often the best time to see the most vibrant coloration.
seasonality.summer: Continues fruiting during humid periods, though colors may fade slightly during dry spells. Look for it after summer rains when other fungi are also active.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for fruiting, with fresh colonies appearing on newly fallen logs and branches. The green color contrasts beautifully with autumn leaves.
seasonality.winter: May persist on logs under snow cover in a dried, less colorful state. Fresh fruiting is rare but possible during winter thaws.

funFact: This fungus contains unique copper-containing compounds called chlorospleniins that create its vivid green color - the same type of chemistry that makes the Statue of Liberty green, but produced naturally by a tiny mushroom!
confusionNotes: The bright green color is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other fungi, but beginners might mistake it for green algae or lichen. Remember: if it's bright green and growing on rotting hardwood in distinct patches, it's almost certainly Green Wood Cup. Algae would be more slimy and lichens would be on bark of living trees or rocks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its small size, this fungus plays an important ecological role as a wood decomposer, helping recycle nutrients back into the forest ecosystem. The genus name is sometimes misspelled as 'Chlorosplenium' in older field guides, but the correct spelling has one 'n'.
compareHints: Green Wood Cup is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique among local fungi for its brilliant green coloration. The closest relatives in appearance would be other small cup fungi like Bisporella citrina (Lemon Disco), but that species is bright yellow rather than green. No other small wood-dwelling fungus in our region displays this distinctive blue-green to yellow-green color.
